title: Global formatting preserves an annotated local date pattern
summary: Under US locale and UTC the local date is stored on the fix while the parent displays the same text from a rejected field. A later valid edit preserves the earlier field error.

change.description: Under US locale and UTC the local date is stored on the fix while the parent displays the same text from a rejected field. A later valid edit preserves the earlier field error.

notes: The exact historical registrar is compiled against the released Framework 5.2.0 graph. Both sides use the subject JVM in UTC. The stored 2009 instant, error count, first field error, rejected text and displayed value are separately observed. This source slice has a distinct evidence scope from a historical Gradle build.

The original JUnit method failed its parent error-count assertion and passed on the landed registrar. The two sides displayed the same local date text. The fix stored epoch millisecond 1256951100000, including after the earlier malformed input. The full historical Gradle build remains unavailable.

On both original registrars the strict checker proved all six converter callbacks and the order of the configured formatters with DateFormatter and DateTimeFormatAnnotationFormatterFactory startup recorded. The fix registers the annotation factory after both the global formatter and the Calendar formatter.

First startup recheck (20261123-011836). Ordinary startup constructs both named thread-local keys and reads the real LocaleContextHolder on both source slices. All four public claims next reach the explicit TimeZone.getTimeZone("UTC") in DateEdits.history. The UTC object and the later bean and error histories still need a native proof.

Both ordinary historical slices now install their named locale context and a fresh mutable UTC zone from the pinned JDK and tzdb. The complete binding claims reach LinkedHashSet construction in GenericConversionService$Converters:502. Both historical registrars now prove their exact callback order from ordinary startup, with and without the global formatter.

Ordinary startup now constructs the ordered converter set and initializes ResolvableType on both formatter slices. All four binding claims first need Class.getGenericInterfaces(). Both historical JVMs resolved the first factory’s source and target to Number and successfully registered it.

Both original default-converter setups register the first Number-to-Number factory from ordinary startup. The native checker preserves the cached generic types when the caller mutates returned arrays and boxes the symbolic ResolvableType hash using the JVM’s shared Integer cache. The full caller next polls a reference queue with a previously registered soft entry.

Both native graphs proved the identity and irreversible loss of one Spring soft-cache entry across purges. Each original JVM completed ten converter registrations before EnumToStringConverter. The full native caller reached its Converter<Enum<?>, String> signature. An independent prefix proof for the first two factories reached the 60-second limit on both sides.
